abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on collaboration among specialized agents to solve complex tasks. Existing methods improve MAS by refining the prompts, skills, and execution strategies of individual agents based on task feedback. However, improving individual agents does not necessarily lead to better team collaboration. Recent studies have therefore extended evolution to the collaboration level, using collective execution experience to adjust team organization, and inter-agent interactions. Nevertheless, evolving collaboration across heterogeneous tasks remains challenging, as existing approaches often constrain team reorganization within a shared structure and reuse interaction rules across incompatible team contexts. In this paper, we propose EvoTeam, a collaboration-centric evolution framework that jointly evolves team organization, interaction rules, and individual agent skills through execution experience. It maintains a library of reusable teams, selecting or creating agent teams and guiding collaboration through team-specific interaction rules. Collaboration experience accumulates within compatible team contexts, while individual skills remain reusable across teams. Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/EvoTeam.

sections.body: The introduction argues that evolving individual agents from execution experience does not necessarily produce better collaborative teams. It names two limits: constrained team reorganization, because existing approaches adjust membership within a shared team, and inappropriate reuse of collaboration experience, because interaction rules tied to one team's responsibilities may introduce unsuitable handoffs or stopping conditions in incompatible contexts. The authors propose EvoTeam with three stages: adaptive agent team composition, team-scoped collaboration, and multi-level experience evolution. Experiments cover four benchmarks and six task categories.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Improving individual agents does not reliably improve team collaboration, so EvoTeam evolves teams, interaction rules, and skills jointly.

sections.body: The preliminary study asks whether experience from earlier tasks helps continued evolution on heterogeneous tasks. Both cross-task settings, Inter-CT with an unsuitable team template and Intra-CT with a compatible template, underperform target-only Meta-Team on all three metrics (Figure 2a). The analysis points to two failure modes: a source-oriented team template that does not support the target division of labor, and inherited interaction rules that prescribe inappropriate handoffs or stopping conditions. The authors conclude that team adaptation should maintain distinct collaboration structures, and that interaction rules should be shared only among tasks with compatible requirements.
sections.heading: Preliminary Study
sections.headline: Reusing experience across heterogeneous tasks underperforms target-only evolution, traced to rigid team templates and inappropriate rule reuse.

sections.body: EvoTeam keeps a global agent pool and a library of reusable teams. Each team has a description of the collaboration requirements it supports and a candidate roster. For each query, a Team Selector reuses a compatible team, and otherwise a Composer creates a provisional team. A Chairman then recruits a task-specific execution team from the roster and assigns subtasks. Agents use their skills and consult the team's interaction rules during execution. After execution, three reflectors update the team roster, the team's rules, and individual agent skills from the composite execution trace. Rules remain team-specific, while skills remain reusable across teams. This section reports no experimental results.
sections.heading: The Framework of EvoTeam
sections.headline: EvoTeam selects or creates task-appropriate teams, coordinates them with team-scoped rules, and evolves teams, rules, and skills.

sections.body: The experiments answer four questions: overall effectiveness, cross-backbone transfer, ablation, and cost. Evaluation covers GAIA, LoCoBench, LOCA-Bench, and BeyondSWE on a common 0 to 100 scale, with GPT-5.6-Luna as the default backbone and avg@3 over three rollouts. Under individual-benchmark evolution, EvoTeam averages 58.85 and leads on four of six metrics. Its GAIA score is 78.00 against 73.00 for Meta-Team. Under mixed-benchmark evolution it averages 59.58, which the text reports as 4.03 points above Meta-Team, and ranks first on all six metrics. Cross-backbone results stay within 4.00 points of same-backbone performance. In the ablation, learned interaction rules add 10.00 points on GAIA and 8.75 on LOCA-Bench.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: EvoTeam scores 58.85 average under individual-benchmark evolution and 59.58 under mixed-benchmark evolution, the highest in each.

sections.body: Related work falls into two strands. Individual agent evolution improves agents through scaffold revision, skill acquisition, and cross-task experience retrieval, but does not by itself resolve responsibility assignment or information exchange during collaboration. Collaborative multi-agent evolution, including Meta-Team, Skill-MAS, and EMAS, adjusts agent behaviors, coordination, and team organization. The authors state that their work focuses on sustaining collaboration evolution across heterogeneous tasks, with coordination experience accumulating within compatible team contexts. Further comparisons appear in Appendix F.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work covers individual agent evolution and collaborative multi-agent evolution, with EvoTeam targeting the latter.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that EvoTeam maintains a library of reusable teams and jointly evolves their organization, team-specific interaction rules, and individual agent skills. Across four benchmarks and six task categories, it leads all six metrics under mixed-benchmark evolution, averaging 59.58 against 55.55 for the strongest baseline. The authors report that cross-backbone evaluations and ablations support the transferability of evolved collaboration experience and the value of jointly evolving team organization and coordination practices.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: EvoTeam averages 59.58 under mixed-benchmark evolution, versus 55.55 for the strongest baseline, with transfer and ablation support.

sections.body: The evaluation does not systematically examine collaborative evolution in multimodal interactive environments, where agents must interpret visual observations and coordinate as the environment changes. The authors note that using multimodal execution traces to refine teams, rules, and skills needs further investigation. EvoTeam also keeps LLM parameters fixed and accumulates experience through explicit updates, so its effectiveness depends on the base model correctly interpreting and applying stored guidance. The authors suggest that combining experience reuse with model adaptation could help internalize frequently useful coordination practices.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Evaluation omits multimodal interactive settings, and results depend on the base model applying stored guidance.

sections.body: The section notes that EvoTeam, like other LLM-based agent systems, may inherit biases from underlying models and produce inaccurate outputs or unintended tool actions. Persistent experience accumulation can retain sensitive information from execution traces and reusable knowledge. The authors recommend access controls, privacy protection, and human oversight for consequential actions in applications beyond the evaluated benchmarks. Accumulated interaction rules and agent skills should be reviewed for suitability before reuse in new contexts, and underlying models, datasets, and tools should respect their licenses and usage policies.
sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.headline: Persistent experience may retain sensitive trace data, so reused rules and skills need review and human oversight.

sections.body: The appendix contains Algorithm 1 for the sequential evolution procedure and details of the GAIA, LoCoBench, LOCA-Bench, BeyondSWE, and mixed-benchmark splits. It gives metric definitions, including the LCBS formula, along with the eight LOCA-Bench task types and the baseline configurations. Prompts for team selection, Chairman coordination, team and agent reflection are included, and the question-and-answer section covers how teams, rules, and evolution work. Case studies illustrate family-scoped updates, cross-benchmark team reuse, and the Carnival refactoring task.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the algorithm, benchmark and metric details, baselines, prompts, questions and answers, and case studies.
